    Shear flow distribution

    Shear flow in AB is a parabolic distribution (CW).

    Shear flow in BC is a positive linear distribution (CCW).

    Shear flow in CD is the sum of a uniform and a parabolic distribution (CCW).

    Shear flow in DA is a negative linear distribution (CCW).

    qA​=qB​=0

    qC​=qD​=16.779 N/mm

    #EST S2 (2020 - 2021)

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    #Part (i)

    Stall boundary is defined by nW=21​ρV2SCLmax​​​.

    Positive limit load boundary is defined by n=3.

    Intersection of the boundaries is the corner point.

    L=nW=21​ρV2SCLmax​​

    3(40000)(9.81)=21​(1.225)(110)2(120)CLmax​​

    CLmax​​=1.3237

    #Part (ii)

    Assume the aircraft is in a steady level flight with gust u=16 m/s.

    Change in angle of attack due to gust,

    Δα=tan−1Vu​≈Vu​

    Small angle approximation.

    Change in lift due to gust,

    ΔL=dαdL​Δα

    ΔL=21​ρV2S⋅dαdCL​​⋅Vu​

    ΔL=21​ρVSCLα​u

    Change in load factor due to gust,

    Δn=WΔL​

    Δn=2WρVSCLα​u​

    Total load factor of level flight,

    n=1+Δn

    n=1+2WρVSCLα​u​

    At point E, V=100 m/s and n=2.4.

    2.4=1+2(40000)(9.81)1.225(100)(120)(16)CLα​​

    CLα​=4.6714/rad

    #Part (iii)

    From the diagram, VB​=110 m/s.

    #Part (c)

    High strength-to-weight ratio:

    • Reduction in weight of the fuselage structure
    • Allows for higher payloads or longer range

    High stiffness/flexural rigidity:

    • Able to resist higher bending loads
    • Minimizes the use of stiffeners in the fuselage structure

    Thermal and acoustic insulation:

    • Low density sandwich core minimizes heat transfer and
      soundwave propagation across the sandwich composite
    • Reduces energy required for air-conditioning
    • Quieter cabin for passengers

    Corrosion resistant (only for fiber composites):

    • Fiber composites, such as CFRP, do not corrode

    #Part (d)

    Wire-braced structures:

    • Aircraft structure consists mainly of trusses
    • Trusses were strengthened by cables held in tension
    • Wire-bracing of trusses were typically oriented diagonally

    Stressed-skin structures:

    • Skin is one of the load-bearing members, including longerons, frames, etc.
    • Stringers transmit loads from the skin to the longerons and frames
    • Stiffeners on the skin increases its buckling strength

    Composite structures:

    • Prepreg fiber composites are applied onto a mold to create the fuselage shape
    • Orientation of each layer differs so as to maximize strength in all directions
    • Reduces the use of fasteners (rivets) to join fuselage sections

    #Part (c)

    Name three types of fuselage shapes used in aircraft. Briefly explain each
    of them, highlighting their advantages, drawbacks, and typical uses.

    Rectangular fuselage shape:

    • Efficient use of internal space (large payload space)
    • Least efficient shape if pressurization is required
    • General aviation aircraft (crop-dusting, leisure, trainer)

    Circular fuselage shape:

    • Most efficient shape if pressurization is required
    • Stress due to pressurization is uniform throughout
    • Payload space is reduced due to curved nature of the shape
    • Most commercial aircraft

    Double lobe fuselage shape:

    • Improves on the space limitation of circular shape
    • Stress concentrations at the intersection of the lobes as cabin
      pressure tends to push the double lobe into a circular shape
    • Cargo aircraft (Lockheed C-5 Galaxy, Antonov An-124, etc.)

    #Part (d)

    What is the wing box? State its function and two structural features.

    Wing box structure:

    • Structural component located in the fuselage that supports wing loads
    • Spars support bending loads while ribs support torsion (twisting)
    • Typically sealed and used as a center fuel tank

    #Part (e)

    Fuselage sections for the A380 are built using GLARE whereas B787 are built using
    carbon fiber reinforced polymers (CFRP) composites. List down six characteristics,
    merits, and demerits, of each of these two materials.

    Fiber-metal laminate (GLARE):

    • Alternating layers of metal and fiber laminates
    • High strength-to-weight ratio
    • High stiffness/flexural rigidity
    • High fatigue resistance
    • Cheaper to manufacture
    • Susceptible to corrosion

    CFRP composites:

    • Fibers (particulate, short or continuous) held together in a resin matrix
    • Multiple layers can be bonded together to form a laminate
    • Laminates can be used to sandwich a honeycomb core
    • High strength-to-weight ratio
    • High stiffness/flexural rigidity
    • Corrosion resistant
    • Defects are not easily detectable as delamination may occur below the surface
    • Requires metal sub-layer for lightning protection as CRFP is an electrical insulator

    #EST S1 (2023 - 2024)

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    Vibrations:

    • Mechanical movement of an object around an equilibrium point
    • An oscillatory motion that repeats itself after an interval of time
    • Occurs when aircraft is subjected to dynamic loads (fluctuating forces)
    • Loads such as turbulence, malfunction of mechanical equipment, etc.
    • Unwanted vibrations can cause fatigue failure of components
      whereby material fails at a load lower than its yield strength
    • Fasteners (nuts and bolts) improperly torqued may loosen and become FOD
    • Passenger comfort will be affected (noise, motion sickness, etc.)

    Gust loads:

    • Sudden, short-lived burst of high-speed wind followed by a lull
    • Gusts change the lift generated by the wings, causing a change in load factor
    • A significant change in load factor can overstress the aircraft’s structure
    • If load factor exceeds ultimate load factor, structural failure may occur
    • Passenger comfort will be affected

    #Part (b)

    • Compliance with regulations as stated by aviation authority
    • Authorities such as Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS)
    • Aircraft must possess a Certificate of Airworthiness (CoA) to operate
    • In addition, aircraft must have a type certificate accepted by authority
    • Maintenance work must be signed off by a Licensed Aircraft Engineer (LAE)

    #Part (c)

    Relief bending loads experienced by the wing:

    • Fuel in the outboard tanks provide a counter-acting moment;
      acting against bending load caused by aerodynamic forces
    • Outboard tanks have a longer moment arm which provides a larger moment
    • Inboard fuel tanks are used first to prolong bending relief provided

    Efficient use of space:

    • Wings cannot be used to carry passengers or cargo
    • Storing fuel in the wings maximizes the available space for payload
    • Payload is revenue generating; higher payload, higher revenue generated

    #Part (b)

    #Part (i)

    Moment of inertia,

    Ixx​=∑Br​yr​2

    Ixx​=2(2000)(300)2+2(2500)(150)2

    Ixx​=472.5×106 mm4

    Note that Ixy​=0 since the section is symmetrical about the x-axis.

    Equation for shear flow,

    qs​−q0​=−Ixx​Sy​​ ∑Br​yr​

    qs​−q0​=−472.5×106100000​ ∑Br​yr​

    qb​=−47251​ ∑Br​yr​

    Cut the section at the wall between booms 1 and 2.
    Analyze as an open section to obtain basic shear flow.

    Basic shear flow

    Shear flow from 1 to 2,

    q12​=0

    Shear flow is zero as it has not passed through a boom.

    Shear flow from 2 to 3,

    q23​=−47251​B2​y2​

    q23​=−47251​(2000)(300)

    q23​=−126.98 N/mm

    Shear flow from 3 to 4,

    q34​=q23​−47251​B3​y3​

    q34​=−126.98−47251​(2000)(−300)

    q34​=0

    Shear flow from 4 to 1,

    q41​=q34​−47251​B4​y4​

    q41​=−47251​(2500)(−150)

    q41​=79.365 N/mm

    Total shear flow

    Since vertical force acts through the shear center, angle of twist ϕ=0.

    Equation for angle of twist,

    ϕ=2A0​G1​∮tqs​​ ds

    0=2A0​G1​∮tqb​​+tq0​​ ds

    q0​=−∮ds/t∮qb​/t ds​

    Evaluating the numerator,

    ∮tqb​​ ds=t23​q23​L23​​+t41​q41​L41​​

    ∮tqb​​ ds=4−126.98(600)​+479.365(300)​

    ∮tqb​​ ds=−13094.625 N/mm

    Evaluating the denominator,

    ∮tds​=t12​L12​​+t23​L23​​+t34​L34​​+t41​L41​​

    ∮tds​=32(1000)​+4600+300​

    ∮tds​=891.67

    Substituting into the angle of twist equation,

    q0​=−891.67−13094.625​

    q0​=14.686 N/mm

    Shear flow direction is anticlockwise.

    Shear flow distribution,

    q12​=14.686 N/mm

    q23​=−126.98+14.686=−112.29 N/mm

    q34​=14.686 N/mm

    q41​=79.365+14.686=94.051 N/mm

    #Part (ii)

    Taking moments about boom 3,

    Sy​e=∮rqs​ ds

    Sy​e=r41​q41​L41​+∫r12​q12​ ds

    Sy​e=r41​q41​L41​+2A12​q12​

    100000e=988.686(94.051)(300)+2[21​(600)(988.686)](14.686)

    e=366.08 mm

    To determine torque due to shear flow q12​, make use
    of the Bredt-Batho equation     T=∫rq ds=2Aq.

    #Part (iii)

    Since vertical forces acts through the shear center, only the applied torque
    causes twisting of the section. Thus, total shear flow would be the sum of
    shear flow due to vertical force, and shear flow due to applied torque.

    From Part (a)(ii),

    Allowable torque based on rate of twist is Tallow​=104146.8 Nm.
    Allowable shear flow is then qtorque​=117042.9 N/m=117.04 N/mm.

    Note that the shear flow due to torque is in the anticlockwise direction.

    Shear flow distribution,

    q12​=14.686+117.04=131.73 N/mm

    q23​=−112.29+117.04=4.75 N/mm

    q34​=q12​=131.73 N/mm

    q41​=94.051+117.04=211.09 N/mm

    ϕ=4A0​2GT​∮t1​ ds

    0.24×180π​=4(0.4449087)2(28×109)T​[0.0032(1)​+0.0040.6+0.3​]
